# Revelation 19: verse-by-verse research notes

**How to read these notes:** Each point gives the page it came from. Commentators' traditions (Wesleyan, Calvinist Baptist, and so on) are given only where the page itself labels them. I ran out of search and fetch calls before I could reach bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, oca.org, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those sections are missing. The Enduring Word page cut off partway through its notes on v. 11, so I have nothing from Guzik on vv. 12–21 except his headings.

---

### Overview: a major difference across the chapter
- **Premillennial reading (vv. 11–21 come before the thousand years):** Constable argues that chapter 20 follows chapter 19 in time. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-20.html. Guzik reads vv. 11–16 as Jesus physically returning to earth, first to the Mount of Olives (Zech 14:3–4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- **Amillennial reading:** Constable notes that many amillennialists view Revelation 20:1-10 as a recapitulation of Revelation 19:11-21. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-20.html. Utley explains what is at stake. If the Second Coming comes before the millennium, some form of pre-millennialism is inevitable. But if chapters 20–22 retell chapters 17–19, then some form of idealism or amillennialism fits best. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21462

---

### vv. 1–5: Praise for Babylon's judgment
**v. 1**
- Guzik links this multitude to the great multitude saved out of the Great Tribulation (7:9–14). "Alleluia" appears four times in this chapter and nowhere else in the New Testament. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Clarke: the word is Hebrew for "praise Jah (Jehovah)". It came into Greek through the Septuagint. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-1.html
- Pulpit Homiletics: "salvation" here means less the forgiveness of sins than being freed from the burden of evil in all its forms. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-19.html

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: this reason for praise matches 16:7 and 15:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Guzik: this is the climax of chapter 18. Babylon's friends mourned her there; God's people celebrate here. The martyrs' cry in 6:10 is finally answered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Pulpit Homiletics: the song expresses burning anger at a moral outrage, which is right. It does not express a desire for revenge, which would be wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-19.html
- **Who is the prostitute?** Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) says she is the false religious system that corrupted the earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-10.html. William Kelly (Brethren) says only Rome fits. In his view "the harlot" stands for her corrupt religion, embracing papal Rome, but not ending with Popery as it is. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-1.html

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: the smoke is from Babylon's burning (18:9, 18). "Forever" shows the judgment is final. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Utley: the line echoes Isaiah 34:10. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-19
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) quotes the view that the verse speaks against universalism. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-19.html

**v. 4**
- Barclay: the 24 elders (twelve patriarchs plus twelve apostles) stand for the whole Church. The four living creatures stand for the best in nature and for the cherubim. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-19.html
- Ironside: this is the elders' last appearance in the book. After this the bride takes their place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/revelation-19.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the voice could be Jesus, but more likely it is an angel who serves at the throne. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Coffman: "small and great" is an idiom meaning all of God's servants. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-19.html

### vv. 6–9: The marriage of the Lamb
**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the multitude is answering the call of v. 5. "Many waters" suggests great power and size. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Guzik, quoting Spurgeon: there is nothing wrong with loud, enthusiastic praise, and half-hearted worship is worthless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/

**v. 7**
- Guzik: in the Old Testament Israel is God's wife; in the New Testament the Church is Christ's betrothed. He quotes Mounce on the two stages of a biblical wedding: betrothal, then the feast. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Pulpit: the bride is the redeemed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm. Conway: it is true both that the Church makes herself ready and that Christ makes her ready. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-19.html

**v. 8: A real Protestant difference over what the "fine linen" is**
- **Common ground (Pulpit):** "it was given her" means the power comes from God, yet she dresses herself willingly. The verse is probably John's comment, not part of the song. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** her white clothing contrasts with the harlot's purple and scarlet. https://biblehub.com/revelation/19-8.htm
- **Gill (Calvinist Baptist):** the linen is not good works, which he says are like filthy rags. It is Christ's righteousness, by which believers are justified. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/revelation/19-8.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** The fine linen here spoken of is not the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers. It is what Christ's grace and Spirit have produced in the saints. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-8.html
- **Matthew Henry:** it is Christ's righteousness, both imputed for justification and imparted for sanctification. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-8.html
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** credited ("imputed") righteousness, received by faith, not a righteousness of works. **Constable (dispensational):** these are the saints' deeds, not their standing before God. Same page.
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** the verse challenges "faith only" teaching. God gave the clothes, but she had to put them on. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-19.html
- **Ligonier devotional (Reformed):** the bride's gown is made of our righteous deeds. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/christs-marriage-supper
- **Conway sermon:** the linen is first put on from outside (Christ our righteousness), then worked out in righteous acts. https://biblehub.com/sermons/revelation/19-8.htm

**v. 9: Who are the guests?**
- Ellicott: the speaker is probably the angel of 17:1. This is one of the book's six beatitudes. https://biblehub.com/revelation/19-9.htm
- Pulpit: the guests are the bride herself, the faithful Church. Same page.
- **Dispensational views:** MacArthur (gty.org) says the bride is the Church. The invited guests are others: Israel, Old Testament believers and tribulation saints. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/66-68/heavenly-hallelujahs-part-3. Ironside sees Israel as the earthly bride and the Church as the heavenly bride, with the supper held in heaven before Christ comes down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/revelation-19.html. Gaebelein says the bride is the Church from Pentecost on, not Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/revelation-19.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist): Christ celebrates the supper as a Lamb, with his Bride the Church. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-marriage-supper-of-the-lamb/
- **Catholic:** the Catechism (CCC 1328, quoted at catholic.com) says the Eucharist anticipates the wedding feast of the Lamb in the heavenly Jerusalem. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/authentic-christian-marriage. A catholic.com audio talk adds that the Church is already the bride, and that the wedding feast is the second stage. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/being-left-behind-in-the-rapture-is-good-actuallyim-serious

### v. 10: John worships the angel
- Guzik: no created being should be worshipped, unlike Jesus, who receives worship. "The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy" means true prophecy always points to Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Pulpit: John does the same thing again later, so he probably did not think the angel was Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican): the angel's correction is indirect evidence that the book is genuine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-10.html
- **Protestant–Catholic debate:**
  - Barnes says the verse rules out worship of Mary or the saints.
  - Clarke (Methodist) says John's bow was only Eastern respect for a superior, not religious worship.
  - Coffman applies it against bowing to the Pope.
  - Haydock (Catholic) answers that Protestants make John himself guilty of the idolatry they charge Catholics with.
  
  All on https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-10.html
- **"Spirit of prophecy":** Barnes says preachers' whole task is to witness to Jesus. Coffman limits the phrase to the apostles, not Christians in general. Barclay calls it ambiguous. Same page.

### vv. 11–16: The rider on the white horse
**v. 11**
- Guzik: this is Jesus returning in power. A horse meant honour, power and speed; white meant victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Precept Austin: because he is faithful he must judge; because he is true he cannot lower God's standards. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-19-commentary
- Bible Hub study notes: this is a different rider from the counterfeit in 6:2, and the verse is a literal picture of the Second Coming. https://biblehub.com/revelation/19-11.htm
- Deffinbaugh: the scene recalls a Roman general's victory parade (the Triumph). https://bible.org/seriespage/26-second-coming-christ-rev-191-21
- Utley: the picture differs from Paul's in 1 Thessalonians 4 and is not a full account of the Second Coming. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21461

**v. 12**
- Coffman: the flaming eyes recall chapter 1 and suggest purity, truth and that he knows everything. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-19.html
- Utley: he wears more crowns than the rider of 6:2 or the dragon of 12:3. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-19
- Biblical Illustrator: a hidden name alongside "Word of God" is a paradox; no one fully knows his nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-16.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: the image comes from Isaiah 63:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Pulpit Homiletics asks whether the blood is his own or his enemies'. Because of Isaiah 63 it concludes it is his enemies'. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-19.html
- Utley: manuscripts differ between "dipped" and "sprinkled", and commentators disagree about what the blood refers to. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-19

**v. 14**
- Deffinbaugh: the armies are the church and the angels. https://bible.org/seriespage/26-second-coming-christ-rev-191-21
- Benson: the white horses show that heaven's people are pure and holy. Biblical Illustrator: no one in the army carries a sword; only the King does. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-16.html

**v. 15**
- Precept Austin: the Greek verb means the sword is coming out right now. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-19-commentary
- Utley: echoes Isaiah 11:4 and Jewish apocalyptic writings. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-19
- Coffman: all three images stand for Christ's word judging, and no actual battle takes place. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-19.html
- Guzik: the rod of iron fulfils Psalm 2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: what "on his thigh" means is uncertain. Alford suggests the name was written partly on the robe and partly on the thigh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): it means the part of the robe over his thigh. Eastern rulers often had titles on their clothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-16.html

### vv. 17–21: The beast defeated
**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik: "flesh" is repeated five times, which is telling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-19/
- Coffman: the scene is symbolic; there are no literal cavalry and no literal feast. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-19.html
- Utley: it echoes two Old Testament battle scenes. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-19

**v. 19**
- Pulpit: the beast is the hostile world power; the kings are the ones gathered in 16:13–14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-19.html
- Ellicott: the Greek says "*the* war". Christ has a single, united army. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/19-16.html
- Bible Hub study notes link this to Armageddon (16:14–16). https://biblehub.com/revelation/19-11.htm

**v. 20**
- Utley: the false prophet is the second beast. His relation to the first beast mimics the Holy Spirit's relation to Christ. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-19
- Pulpit: this is the destruction of Satan's earthly instruments, the hostile world power and self-deception. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: "the rest" are the beast's followers. The birds feeding stresses the disgrace done to their bodies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/19.htm
- Precept Austin (dispensational) links this to the judgment of the nations in Matthew 25. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-19-commentary
